guides.dek: Muse is the most common personal AI agent on sites that use Verisoul, and it never says who it is.
guides.answer: You can't detect Meta Muse by its user agent or IP address, because it browses from Meta's cloud as ordinary desktop Chrome on Linux and Meta publishes no user agent token, signature or IP list for it. You detect it by combining the hosting network it exits through, the cloud virtual machine its browser runs on and session behavior no person produces. Verisoul does this automatically and returns agent id meta_muse.

body.text: Meta Muse is the personal AI agent people are pointing at your website most often right now. Across sites that use Verisoul, Muse made up 68% of the personal-agent sessions we named between Oct 29 and Nov 1, 2026, its first days in our API, which is about five times as many as the next agent, Instinct. It was also the most widespread, appearing on about 2.5 times as many customer sites as OpenAI's cloud browser, the next most widespread agent, and its volume stayed at a similar level each day after the first.

Meta launched Muse on Sep 8, 2026 in the US on iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp, and it climbed to No. 1 among free apps on the US App Store on Sep 18. [TechCrunch reported](https://techcrunch.com/2026/09/25/meta-is-putting-its-muscle-behind-muse-as-the-ai-app-takes-off) about 2.8 million downloads in its first two weeks. Muse takes a goal, makes a plan and keeps working in the background, which in practice means it signs in to accounts, fills forms, compares prices and checks out for its user. It asks for approval before it buys anything or sends an email, so on an iPhone the last thing the user sees before Muse reaches your checkout is a prompt asking to place the order with a saved card.

Site owners started asking about it after Amazon blocked Muse in September 2026. [Amazon said](https://thenewstack.io/amazon-meta-muse-block/) Meta never disclosed the access, the agent didn't identify itself and it appeared to store customer credentials, a claim Meta disputes. Every team that runs a login page, a checkout or a sign-up flow now has the same question: how much of this traffic is Muse, and what should we do about it?
How Meta Muse shows up on your site

According to [Meta's launch post](https://about.fb.com/news/2026/09/introducing-muse-personal-ai-agent/), every Muse user gets a dedicated virtual machine in Meta's cloud running its own Chromium browser, and a separate safety agent on that machine approves outbound traffic through an egress proxy. When Muse visits your site, you are talking to that cloud browser. It loads pages, runs your JavaScript and submits forms the way a real browser does, because it is one. At Meta Connect on Sep 23, 2026, Meta also announced that Muse can operate a Mac, where it asks permission before actions such as moving files to the Trash.

What it does not do is announce itself. The browser reports as ordinary desktop Chrome on Linux with no AI token, and its traffic exits through large CDN networks instead of the consumer ISPs a shopper's phone or laptop would use. Meta documents robots.txt and user agents for its crawlers, such as Meta-ExternalAgent and Meta-WebIndexer, and says nothing comparable for Muse, even though Muse produced roughly 20 times as many sessions as Meta-ExternalAds across sites that use Verisoul in the same window.

body.text: Why Muse is hard to detect

Most agent detection starts with a declaration you can match or verify: a token in the user agent, a published IP file or a Web Bot Auth signature that proves who sent the request. Muse gives you none of these, so allowlists and user agent rules have nothing to match, while a static IP or browser rule only lasts until Meta changes the egress or the browser. Amazon's block was reportedly bypassed that way, by running Firefox through Muse's egress proxy.

The browser itself does not help much either. A real Chromium instance in a real virtual machine doesn't carry the headless markers that cheap scrapers leave behind, and because Muse often signs in with its user's own credentials, a Muse session on an existing account can look a lot like account takeover from a new device. The signal is in the combination: where the session comes from, what kind of machine it runs on and how it moves through the page.
How Verisoul detects Meta Muse

Verisoul names Muse by inference, which means we combine several independent signals because there is no declaration to check. On the network side, the traffic exits through the hosting network Muse runs on and carries a bot-like network score. On the device side, the browser is cloud hosted with a virtual machine device profile. On the behavior side, the session shows bot-like interaction patterns from start to finish. No single one of these says Muse on its own, while together they do, and Verisoul returns the result in the API next to the bot score.

items: `id` is the stable name you write rules against, here `meta_muse`
`type` is `ai_assistant`, meaning an agent acting for one person, as opposed to a crawler or a headless scraper
`detection_method` is `inferred`, which tells you Verisoul identified the agent from evidence and did not rely on a signature or a self-declared user agent
`detection_signals` lists the signal families that agreed, here `network`, `device` and `behavioral`

body.text: The [Agent Atlas entry for Meta Muse](https://www.verisoul.ai/agents/meta-muse) shows the same response and the signals behind it, and the [AI agent detection docs](https://docs.verisoul.ai) explain every method and field.
How to detect Meta Muse step by step

items: Add Verisoul to the pages where agents act, such as sign-up, login, checkout and payouts, so every session gets a bot score and an agent field
Read the `agent` object in each Verisoul API response and log `meta_muse` sessions separately for a week to see where Muse shows up in your flows
Write a rule for the `meta_muse` id in your decision engine for each step, using the [AI agent detection docs](https://docs.verisoul.ai) as the field reference
Send Muse sessions on risky steps, such as new accounts, payout changes and password resets, to step-up checks or manual review

body.text: Should you block Meta Muse?

Usually not everywhere. Muse acts for a real, often paying person, so blocking it outright at browse and checkout can cost you customers who simply asked their agent to buy something. Most teams let Muse browse and complete purchases and treat it as a known agent instead of an unknown bot.

The steps that deserve friction are the ones where fraud pays: creating new accounts, claiming sign-up bonuses, changing payout details and resetting passwords. An agent that can run many sessions in parallel from cloud machines makes those steps easier to abuse, so review or step-up checks there protect you without turning away legitimate shoppers.

faq.q: Does Meta Muse identify itself to websites?
faq.a: No. Muse reports as ordinary desktop Chrome on Linux, and Meta publishes no user agent token, Web Bot Auth signature or IP list for it. Amazon cited this when it blocked Muse in September 2026.

faq.q: Why did Amazon block Meta Muse?
faq.a: Amazon said Meta never disclosed the access, the agent didn't identify itself and it appeared to store customer credentials. Meta disputes the credential claim.

faq.q: How do I block Meta Muse from my website?
faq.a: A robots.txt rule or a user agent rule won't work because Muse doesn't declare itself. Use detection that infers it from network, device and behavior, such as Verisoul's meta_muse label, and apply your rule to that label.

faq.q: How common is Meta Muse traffic?
faq.a: Across sites that use Verisoul, Muse made up 68% of the personal-agent sessions we named between Oct 29 and Nov 1, 2026, about five times as many as the next agent, and it appeared on about 2.5 times as many customer sites as the next most widespread agent.

faq.q: Should I block Muse or let it through?
faq.a: It depends on the step. Muse usually works for a real customer, so most teams let it browse and buy and add friction at account creation, payouts and account changes.

guides.dek: OpenAI's always-on dots browse from a cloud browser that OpenAI signs, so verified sessions are easy to name.
guides.answer: You detect ChatGPT dots by verifying the Web Bot Auth signature on requests from OpenAI's cloud browser, which OpenAI signs as chatgpt.com, because the user agent carries no dots or AI token. OpenAI documents that signing for its ChatGPT cloud browser and its dots docs don't say whether every dot uses it, while dots working through a user's own computer look like that person's browser. When the signature verifies, Verisoul returns agent id chatgpt_agent.

body.text: Dots are OpenAI's always-on personal agents inside ChatGPT. OpenAI launched them at DevDay on Sep 29, 2026 for ChatGPT Pro and Business Premium, with Enterprise, Edu and Healthcare in an admin-enabled beta. A dot pursues a goal in the background around the clock, using its own cloud computer and browser plus thousands of app plugins, and checks in with its user for approval. The [dots docs](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/dots) show examples like drafting invoices, background research and filling in a DMV registration.

Across sites that use Verisoul, OpenAI's cloud browser, which we name `chatgpt_agent`, made up 13% of the personal-agent sessions we named between Oct 29 and Nov 1, 2026, and it was the most widespread agent after Meta Muse, appearing on about 40% as many customer sites as Muse. That id covers signed traffic from OpenAI's cloud browser in general, so it includes dots without being limited to them.

The naming is confusing for a reason. ChatGPT agent, OpenAI's earlier agent mode, was removed from ChatGPT in early August 2026 and its tasks were split across ChatGPT Work, its cloud browser and Codex. Dots now run on that same kind of cloud computer, which is why the traffic still looks like what fraud teams used to call ChatGPT agent.
How ChatGPT dots show up on your site

Each dot has its own computer and browser in OpenAI's cloud that keeps working while the user's devices are off, and the user can open it and take over at any point. A dot can also use one connected personal computer running the ChatGPT app, in which case its traffic leaves from that person's own network in that person's own browser.

For the cloud browser, OpenAI's [allowlisting help article](https://help-lb.openai.com/en/articles/11845367-chatgpt-works-cloud-browser-allowlisting) says requests are signed with Web Bot Auth, with a `Signature-Agent` of `https://chatgpt.com` and public keys at `chatgpt.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory`. That article covers the ChatGPT Work cloud browser and doesn't mention dots by name. Cloudflare also included ChatGPT agent in the first group of [signed agents](https://blog.cloudflare.com/signed-agents/) it recognizes by their Web Bot Auth signatures, so sites behind Cloudflare can already act on that identity. The user agent itself reports as ordinary Chrome on Linux with no dots or AI token.

body.text: Why dots are only medium hard to detect

When the cloud browser signs, detection is straightforward: you verify the signature against OpenAI's published keys and you know the request came from OpenAI, which is much stronger than any user agent match because a signature can't be copied. A `Signature-Agent` header without a valid signature is only a claim, so verification is the step that matters.

The hard part is everything outside that path. OpenAI's dots docs don't confirm that every dot signs, so unsigned dot traffic is possible, while a dot routed through a user's connected computer arrives from a home IP in a normal browser and carries no OpenAI identity at all. Those sessions need the same device and behavior analysis you would use for an undeclared agent.
How Verisoul detects ChatGPT dots

For signed sessions, Verisoul verifies the Web Bot Auth signature against OpenAI's chatgpt.com key, which is the cryptographic signal. We then check that the device is a cloud-hosted browser with a virtual machine profile and that clicks, typing and page flow are automated instead of a person's. When all three line up, the API names the session.

items: `id` is `chatgpt_agent`, the stable name for OpenAI's signed cloud browser, which dots use when they browse from the cloud
`type` is `ai_agent`, an agent doing multi-step work in its own browser
`detection_method` is `signed`, meaning a verified cryptographic signature identified the operator
`detection_signals` lists `cryptographic`, `device` and `behavioral`, the three checks that agreed

body.text: Unsigned or laptop-routed dots are not named, and Verisoul scores those sessions through bot score instead. The [Agent Atlas entry](https://www.verisoul.ai/agents/chatgpt-agent) shows the sample response, and the [AI agent detection docs](https://docs.verisoul.ai) cover each method.
How to detect ChatGPT dots step by step

items: Turn on Verisoul on sign-up, login, checkout and account pages so each session returns a bot score and an agent field
Filter API responses for `agent.id` equal to `chatgpt_agent` and check that `detection_method` is `signed`
Write one rule for verified `chatgpt_agent` sessions and a separate bot score rule for unnamed automation, using the [AI agent detection docs](https://docs.verisoul.ai)
Route dots on sign-up, payouts and password changes to review, and let them browse and sign in elsewhere

body.text: Should you block ChatGPT dots?

Dots work for paying ChatGPT subscribers, so blocking verified sessions mostly turns away real customers. Most teams allow signed sessions to browse, sign in and fill forms, since the signature gives a clear, accountable operator behind the request.

New accounts, payouts and credential changes are different, because an always-on agent can repeat those steps at a pace no person would. Review or step-up there, and treat unsigned automation by its bot score rather than by any OpenAI claim in a header.

faq.q: Does OpenAI dots identify itself to websites?
faq.a: Partly. The user agent is ordinary Chrome on Linux with no AI token, while OpenAI signs its cloud browser's requests with Web Bot Auth as chatgpt.com. OpenAI's dots docs don't say whether every dot uses that signing.

faq.q: Do dots sign requests with Web Bot Auth like ChatGPT agent?
faq.a: OpenAI documents Web Bot Auth for its ChatGPT cloud browser, with keys at chatgpt.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory. Confirm in your own logs whether your dot traffic carries a valid signature.

faq.q: What happened to ChatGPT agent mode?
faq.a: ChatGPT agent was removed from ChatGPT in early August 2026 and its tasks were split across ChatGPT Work, its cloud browser and Codex. Verisoul still names OpenAI's signed cloud browser chatgpt_agent.

faq.q: How do I allow or block ChatGPT dots on my site?
faq.a: Write your rule on the verified chatgpt.com signature or on Verisoul's chatgpt_agent id, because the user agent is plain Chrome. A Signature-Agent header without a valid signature proves nothing.

faq.q: Why can't I use dots in the UK or EU?
faq.a: OpenAI offers dots on ChatGPT Pro only to adults outside the EEA, UK and Switzerland. Business Premium accounts can use dots worldwide.

guides.answer: You detect Claude Duet by its user agent, because Anthropic says Duet's cloud browser sends a distinct User-Agent, observed in production as Linux Chrome with a Claude-Agent/1.0 token. Anthropic documents no Web Bot Auth signature for Duet, so the token can be copied and should be checked against the network and behavior of the session. body.text: Claude Duet is Anthropic's proactive agent app. It launched on Oct 21, 2026 as a waitlist research preview for US Claude Pro and Max subscribers, on iOS, Android and claude.ai. Duet watches the work apps a user connects, sends a morning brief and finishes tasks in the background on its own cloud computer, such as scheduling meetings, chasing unpaid invoices, running payroll or setting up a Shopify store. It asks for approval before it sends, pays, signs or deletes anything.

It is still early. Across sites that use Verisoul, `claude_duet` made up under 1% of the personal-agent sessions we named between Oct 29 and Nov 1, 2026. Anthropic's other browsing agent shows up more often: the Claude desktop app's browser made up 3% in the same window, and Verisoul names it separately as `claude_desktop`.

Duet matters anyway because of how it is built. It signs in, buys with one-time virtual cards and does business admin, which puts it on exactly the pages fraud teams care about, and its waitlist will open up.
How Claude Duet shows up on your site

Duet's browser runs in a dedicated cloud virtual machine kept separate from the model, which controls it only through open, click and type commands. Cookies stay on the browser machine, and users can't watch or take over the browser yet. Anthropic's [safety, privacy and security article](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-duet-safety-privacy-and-security) says the browser sends a distinct User-Agent and that Anthropic publishes the IP addresses Duet browses from, though the article doesn't link the list.

The exact string has been seen in the wild. A [GitHub issue on Adobe's RUM collector](https://github.com/adobe/helix-rum-collector/issues/668) from Oct 30, 2026 recorded `Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko; compatible; Claude-Agent/1.0) Chrome/156.0.0.0 Safari/537.36` in production traffic, and generic parsers had been reading it as plain Linux desktop Chrome.

body.text: Why Claude Duet is easy to detect, with one catch

Duet declares itself, which already puts it ahead of most personal agents. A plain string match on `Claude-Agent/` catches honest Duet traffic, and Anthropic also contacted several large sites before launch and let them opt out, which shows it expects sites to make decisions about it.

The catch is that a user agent is a claim, while a signature is proof. Without a documented Web Bot Auth signature, anyone can paste `Claude-Agent/1.0` into a script, so a match should be confirmed against the source network and the session's behavior before you trust it. Keep Duet separate from ClaudeBot, Claude-User and Claude-SearchBot as well, since those are Anthropic's crawlers and fetchers with their own rules.
How Verisoul detects Claude Duet

Verisoul treats Duet as self-declared and then checks the declaration. The network signal confirms the source IP belongs to the operator's own network, and the behavioral signal confirms automated clicks, typing and page flow instead of a person's. A `Claude-Agent` string arriving from the wrong network or with human-looking input is treated as a spoof, and device signals are added when automation flags show in the browser.

items: `id` is `claude_duet`, the name to put in your rules
`type` is `ai_assistant`, an agent acting for one person
`detection_method` is `self_declared`, meaning Duet announced itself and Verisoul verified that announcement
`detection_signals` lists `network` and `behavioral`, the two checks that confirmed it

body.text: See the [Agent Atlas entry for Claude Duet](https://www.verisoul.ai/agents/claude-duet) for the sample response and the [AI agent detection docs](https://docs.verisoul.ai) for the full list of methods.
How to detect Claude Duet step by step

items: Install Verisoul on sign-up, login and checkout so every session returns an agent field next to the bot score
Look for `agent.id` equal to `claude_duet`, and keep `claude_desktop` sessions in a separate bucket
Write a rule per id in your decision engine and treat a `Claude-Agent` user agent that Verisoul doesn't confirm as suspicious
Review Duet on account creation, payouts and account changes, where an agent's speed matters most

body.text: Should you block Claude Duet?

Duet acts for a paying Claude subscriber and asks before it pays or sends anything, so most teams allow it to browse and check out. It signs in through an encrypted password form on the user's device that the model never sees, and it pays with Link one-time virtual cards or Shop Pay, which limits how far a mistake can go.

Add review on sign-up, payouts and account changes, and treat a Claude-Agent user agent from the wrong network as a spoof. If you would rather keep Duet off your site entirely, a rule on the `claude_duet` id does that without touching Anthropic's crawlers.

faq.q: What user agent does Claude Duet use?
faq.a: Production traffic has shown Mozilla/5.0 (X11; Linux x86_64) AppleWebKit/537.36 (KHTML, like Gecko; compatible; Claude-Agent/1.0) Chrome/156.0.0.0 Safari/537.36, per a GitHub issue from Oct 30, 2026. Anthropic confirms Duet sends a distinct user agent, though its docs don't print the string.

faq.q: How do I block Claude Duet from my site?
faq.a: Match the Claude-Agent token, or use a detection label such as Verisoul's claude_duet, and apply your rule to that. Anthropic also let several large sites opt out before launch.

faq.q: Does Claude Duet respect robots.txt?
faq.a: Anthropic says Duet aims to follow the rules sites set for agents, though it hasn't published the details. Its robots.txt docs cover only ClaudeBot, Claude-User and Claude-SearchBot.

faq.q: Can Claude Duet buy things on websites?
faq.a: Yes, with the user's approval. It pays with Link one-time virtual cards or Shop Pay and signs in through a password form on the user's device, and it can't trade securities or move money between accounts.

faq.q: Is Claude Duet the same as the Claude desktop app?
faq.a: No. Duet browses from its own cloud computer, while the Claude desktop app browses from the person's own machine. Verisoul names them separately as claude_duet and claude_desktop.

body.text: Grok Bot is xAI's always-on agent product. Each Bot is a persistent, named AI teammate that works on a cloud computer with a browser, terminal and files, signing in to the user's apps and websites to run multi-step jobs and routines. xAI, renamed SpaceXAI in July 2026, launched it in beta on Aug 11, 2026 for SuperGrok and Cursor paid plans, included it with all SuperGrok, Cursor Pro and Cursor Teams plans on Aug 26 and opened it to enterprises on Sep 3, when the waitlist ended.

The [Grok Bot docs](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot) describe use cases that land squarely on business websites: sales prospecting and CRM cleanup, inbox and subscription cleanup, customer support refunds, invoice and expense processing and checkout with saved cards, Link or X Money. A Bot has no identity of its own and acts as the signed-in member, which is why fraud and risk teams need to tell it apart from that member typing by hand.
xAI has not published usage numbers, and Verisoul does not have enough named Grok Bot traffic yet to report volumes.
How Grok Bot shows up on your site

Each member gets one microVM in Cursor's cloud in the US, shared by all of their Bots, with a browser, filesystem, terminal and persistent browser sessions. By default those computers leave through shared static egress IPs used by every Grok Bot customer, which xAI gives out only through its account team. Users can also turn on a setting called Route traffic through this computer, after which your site sees their desktop's connection instead of the hosted computer's IP.

xAI's [security docs](https://docs.x.ai/grok-bot/security) say Bots should hand CAPTCHAs, blocks and human checks back to the user instead of working around them, and that some services flag datacenter IPs.

xAI's docs don't mention signing, while [Cloudflare Radar's bot directory](https://radar.cloudflare.com/bots/directory/grok-bot) lists Grok Bot as a signed agent with a published Web Bot Auth key directory under a GrokAgent user agent pattern. That gives sites a way to verify Grok Bot cryptographically, and sites behind Cloudflare can act on the signed identity directly.

Verisoul verifies the signed request cryptographically against the provider's key, then checks that the browser is cloud hosted with a virtual machine device profile and that clicks, typing and page flow are automated. A signature tells you who operated the request, and the device and behavior checks confirm the session matches it.

body.text: Why Instinct is hard to detect

With no user agent, signature or IP list, there is nothing to match or verify, so allowlists and signature checks see an ordinary browser. Instinct isn't listed in Cloudflare's signed agent or verified bot directories either, so sites behind Cloudflare get no named identity for it. The usual free hints, such as a logged-in session arriving from a cloud network instead of the customer's home or mobile carrier, fit Instinct but also fit every other cloud automation tool and plenty of VPN users.

The credential problem makes it worse. Because Instinct often signs in as the real user, the risk signals that would flag a stranger, like a correct password on a new device, fire on a legitimate customer's own errand. Teams that can't tell Instinct apart from an attacker end up either blocking their customers or loosening rules that catch real takeovers.
How Verisoul detects Instinct

Verisoul names Instinct by inference from two signal families. On the device side, the browser runs on a cloud GPU with an operating system and font profile that don't match each other, plus a fixed rendering fingerprint. On the behavior side, it clicks without moving the mouse and fills forms without typing. Each is unusual on its own, and together they identify Instinct's cloud browser even when the credentials are perfect.

Instinct acts for a real person with their own logins and cards, so blocking it can cost you customers, especially in travel, ticketing, restaurants and retail where it does most of its errands. Most teams allow it to browse and buy and label it so it doesn't trip account takeover rules.

body.text: Hark is a consumer AI assistant from Hark Labs, the company founded by Brett Adcock. Its Handoff agent runs a cloud computer with real browsers that sign in to sites and finish web tasks for the user, such as paying bills, cancelling subscriptions, shopping and topping up cards. Hark previewed Handoff on Aug 5, 2026 and made Hark Pro free on web, iOS and Android on Oct 6, 2026, with Handoff as its cloud computer and paid tiers at $20 and $100 a month for more usage.

Adoption arrived fast. Hark reported 130,208 Handoff browser sessions and 143,244 daily active users in the first 24 hours after the free launch, figures [the company shared publicly](https://postcutoff.com/e/2026-10-06-hark-launches-personal-ai-assistant/) and that have not been independently checked. Verisoul does not have enough named HarkBot traffic yet to report volumes.
Hark also stands out for a better reason: it is one of the few consumer agents that publishes all three identity signals a site owner can check.
How Hark shows up on your site

Each Handoff request gets a dedicated virtual computer with its own browser, file system and terminal, and the model drives it with cursor and keyboard actions. Handoff can run up to six browsers at once, users can watch a live view, and credentials sit in a vault Hark calls Secured by Hark. Hark's terms say it normally asks for confirmation before spending money or sending messages.

Hark's [bot documentation](https://app.hark.com/about/bot) describes HarkBot as a user-initiated fetcher that sends `HarkBot/1.0`, signs with Web Bot Auth using an Ed25519 key published at `hark.com/.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory`, and comes from IP ranges listed at `hark.com/agent/ipranges/harkbot.json`. Hark says to refetch that file rather than pin it. [Cloudflare Radar](https://radar.cloudflare.com/bots/directory/harkbot) lists HarkBot as a verified bot with that signature directory, so sites behind Cloudflare can allow or block it by name. What the docs don't say is whether full interactive Handoff browser sessions send the same identity.

body.text: Gemini Agent is Google's agent inside the Gemini app. It takes multi-step actions for a user, such as preparing a car rental or travel booking, handling Gmail and Calendar tasks, filling forms and browsing sites, and it asks before it sends email or buys anything. Google launched it for AI Ultra subscribers in the US on Nov 18, 2025. Gemini Spark, announced at Google I/O on May 19, 2026, is the always-on version that keeps working in the background on dedicated Google Cloud virtual machines, and it reached AI Pro subscribers in the US and more than 160 other countries on Jul 30, 2026.

Across sites that use Verisoul, the `google_agent` id made up about 1% of the personal-agent sessions we named between Oct 29 and Nov 1, 2026. Google's assistive traffic shows up in much larger numbers elsewhere: Google Read Aloud, a text-to-speech fetcher and not a personal agent, produced about twice as many sessions as Meta Muse in the same window, which is a reminder to keep Google's agents, fetchers and crawlers in separate rules.
Google retired its earlier agent experiment, Project Mariner, on May 4, 2026 and folded its capabilities into Gemini Agent and Chrome auto browse.
How Gemini Agent shows up on your site

When Gemini works from Google's cloud, it uses a remote browser that identifies itself. Google's [Google-Agent documentation](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-agent) describes a Chrome on Linux user agent with a `compatible; Google-Agent` token and a link back to the docs, plus a mobile variant, for agents hosted on Google infrastructure. Google added Google-Agent to its list of user-triggered fetchers on Mar 23, 2026 and publishes the IP ranges in `user-triggered-agents.json`.

Google also [signs some Google-Agent requests](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/web-bot-auth) with Web Bot Auth as `agent.bot.goog`, which it describes as experimental and limited to a subset of requests. Spark is different when it drives the user's own desktop Chrome, a mode added on Jul 30, 2026: those sessions use the person's browser and logins and carry no Google-Agent token.

body.text: Why Gemini Agent is easy to detect in the cloud

Cloud sessions line up three ways: the user agent token, a published IP list with reverse DNS ending in `gae.googleusercontent.com` or `google.com`, and a partial signature. Google itself warns that user agent strings can be spoofed, so the IP or signature check is what turns a claim into proof. A missing signature doesn't prove a fake, because Google only signs a subset.

The blind spot is local mode. When Spark drives a person's own Chrome, there is no Google-Agent token and no Google IP, so the session looks like that person browsing. Google's docs also say Google-Agent covers agents on its infrastructure without naming Gemini Agent or Spark specifically, so treat the id as Google's agent traffic as a whole.
How Verisoul detects Gemini Agent

Verisoul treats Google-Agent as self-declared and then verifies it. The network signal confirms the source IP belongs to Google's published ranges, the device signal confirms a cloud-hosted browser with a virtual machine profile, and the behavioral signal confirms automated clicks, typing and page flow. A Google-Agent string from outside Google's network fails that check.

body.text: Should you block Gemini Agent?

Gemini acts for a signed-in Google user and asks before purchases, so most teams allow verified Google-Agent sessions to browse and buy. Blocking Google-Agent also doesn't affect search indexing, because it is separate from Googlebot, so the decision is purely about the agent.

Review sign-up and payouts, where an always-on agent can repeat actions at scale. Spark sessions in a user's local Chrome are not named and fall back to Verisoul's bot score, so keep a score-based rule for those steps too.

faq.a: Google-Agent is the user agent Google uses for agents hosted on its infrastructure when they visit a site for a person, which is how Gemini's cloud agent sessions are expected to appear. Google added it to its user-triggered fetchers list on Mar 23, 2026.

faq.a: No. Google-Agent is separate from Googlebot, so blocking it does not affect search indexing.

faq.a: Generally no. Google says user-triggered fetchers ignore robots.txt because a person asked for the fetch, so use a user agent, IP or detection rule instead.

You detect it from what the session looks like and how it behaves, such as a cloud browser on a logged-in account and automated input, while its Mac app and Chrome extension modes run in the user's own browser. body.text: Perplexity Computer is Perplexity's general-purpose agent, which the company describes as a digital worker. It coordinates several AI models to run multi-step projects end to end, such as research and report building, filling out forms, shopping and long-running monitoring, using a real browser, filesystem and tool integrations in an isolated environment. Perplexity [launched it on Feb 25, 2026](https://www.perplexity.ai/hub/blog/introducing-perplexity-computer) for Perplexity Max subscribers, a plan [MacRumors puts](https://www.macrumors.com/2026/04/16/perplexity-personal-computer-for-mac/) at $200 a month.

Two later releases moved it closer to the user. Personal Computer for Mac rolled out on Apr 16, 2026 and combines a Mac with Perplexity's server environments, and since Oct 30, 2026 a Chrome extension lets the Mac and Windows apps work inside the user's own signed-in tabs in Chrome, Edge, Brave and Arc.

Shopping agents from Perplexity have also been to court. Amazon sued over Perplexity's Comet browser agent shopping on Amazon, [won a preliminary injunction in March 2026](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/03/10/amazon-wins-court-order-to-block-perplexitys-ai-shopping-agent.html), and saw the Ninth Circuit vacate it on Aug 4, 2026, holding that the human user, not the agent's developer, accesses the site. Perplexity has not published usage numbers for Computer, and Verisoul does not name it yet, so we have no volumes to report.
How Perplexity Computer shows up on your site

Each Computer task runs in an isolated environment on Perplexity's servers with a real browser and filesystem, and it uses the same interfaces a person does. Perplexity's [crawler documentation](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/resources/perplexity-crawlers) covers only two agents: PerplexityBot, its crawler, and Perplexity-User, the fetcher that grabs a page when someone asks Perplexity about it. Neither describes Computer's browser.
In extension and Mac modes, Computer works in the user's real browser on their home network, so it carries their cookies, their IP and their device.
Why Perplexity Computer is hard to detect

There is nothing to match. Perplexity-User declares itself and comes from a published IP file, which makes Perplexity's simple page fetches easy to name, while Computer's cloud browser has no documented token, signature or IP list. A rule written for Perplexity-User will not catch it.

Perplexity's track record is another reason not to wait for it to declare itself. On Aug 4, 2025, [Cloudflare reported](https://blog.cloudflare.com/perplexity-is-using-stealth-undeclared-crawlers-to-evade-website-no-crawl-directives/) that when Perplexity's declared crawlers were blocked, an undeclared crawler posing as Chrome on macOS fetched the same pages from unlisted IPs that rotated across networks, about 3 to 6 million requests a day next to 20 to 25 million from its declared agents, and removed Perplexity from its verified bots. Perplexity disputed the finding and said the traffic came from BrowserBase, a hosted browser service it uses. That story concerns Perplexity's fetchers, not Computer, but it shows why a rule that waits for a Perplexity token can miss Perplexity traffic.

The local modes make it harder still, because IP and user agent checks see a normal user in a normal browser. What remains is the session itself. [Academic work on AI browsing agents](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.01247v1), studied on Perplexity's Comet rather than Computer, found tells such as text pasted programmatically instead of typed, pointer jumps straight to click targets and short bursts of scrolling, and those are the kinds of signals that still work when the network and user agent look human.
How Verisoul detects Perplexity Computer

Verisoul does not yet name Perplexity Computer, and we would rather say so than guess. Its sessions still get caught: cloud browser and automation markers in the device count toward the bot score, as do automated clicks, typing and navigation. Perplexity's separate page fetches declare Perplexity-User, and Verisoul names those `perplexity_user`. A Computer session today looks like this in the API.

When a session is named, the `agent` object carries `id`, `type`, `detection_method` and `detection_signals`, as described in the docs

body.text: Manus is a general-purpose AI agent from Butterfly Effect, a Singapore company, that takes a task from a user and runs it on its own cloud computer, browsing, researching, filling forms and building documents or apps along the way. It opened as an invite-only preview on Mar 6, 2025 and to public registration on May 13, 2025, and it has since added a Browser Operator extension (Nov 18, 2025) that lets the agent work inside the user's own browser, plus a desktop app.

The company has had an unusual year. Meta announced a deal to buy Manus in Dec 2025, China ordered it withdrawn on Apr 27, 2026, and Manus has run independently since Sep 1, 2026. On Sep 28, 2026 it launched Manus 2.0 and the Cue app, which give agents their own email addresses, phone numbers, wallets and computers, and on Oct 8, 2026 it raised over $500M led by Boyu Capital and IDG Capital. One public real user monitoring dataset on GitHub counted 9,000 to 20,000 Manus requests a day across 224 to 341 sites in the week of Oct 24, 2026, which its authors call a lower bound.

Site owners ask about Manus for two reasons. Its users send it to do real work like research and bookings, and the same agent is good at scraping and at creating accounts, which the new Cue identities make easier.
How Manus shows up on your site

In its default cloud mode, Manus browses from an isolated virtual computer. Researchers at UC Davis found about 96.6% of the Manus tasks they studied ran Linux Chromium with the clock set to UTC, and the GitHub study traced the traffic to Google Cloud. The user agent is a normal Linux Chrome string with `Manus-User/1.0` appended, and page loads carry a Web Bot Auth signature naming `https://api.manus.im`, with the Ed25519 public key published in Manus's own key directory. [Cloudflare Radar](https://radar.cloudflare.com/bots/directory/manus-bot) lists the agent in its bot directory as Manus Bot and points to that same key directory, which is a useful cross-check that the signature belongs to Manus.

body.text: Browser Operator and the desktop app behave differently, because they drive the user's own browser on the user's own network and carry no Manus token at all.
Why Manus is only partly easy to detect

Cloud Manus is one of the more honest agents on the web, since it declares itself in the user agent and signs its requests. The catch is in the details. The GitHub study saw signatures on page loads only, while scripts, beacons and other subresource requests from the same session went out unsigned, so a check that runs on every request will see a signed page followed by a string of unsigned calls from the same visitor. There is also no IP list to confirm the network, which leaves the signature as the only proof of identity.

The local modes are harder. When a user runs Manus through Browser Operator, the requests come from their real browser, cookies and home IP, and the only remaining clue is how the agent behaves on the page. The UC Davis researchers saw Manus jump the scroll position instantly, teleport the pointer to click targets and type far faster than a person.
How Verisoul detects Manus

Verisoul names Manus by verifying its Web Bot Auth signature against the key Manus publishes, which proves the request came from Manus and not from a scraper copying its user agent. We then tie that signed page load to the rest of the session, so unsigned scripts and beacons inherit the identity, and we check that the device and behavior match a cloud agent.

body.text: ChatGPT Atlas was OpenAI's AI browser, a Chromium-based browser for macOS with ChatGPT built in. It launched on Oct 21, 2025, and its agent mode, a preview for Plus, Pro and Business users, could navigate, click and finish multi-step tasks like booking an appointment or filling a grocery cart inside the user's own browser. OpenAI said in March 2026 that it would fold Atlas, the ChatGPT desktop app and Codex into one desktop app, announced the retirement on Jul 9, 2026 and shut Atlas down on Aug 9, 2026, less than ten months after launch. The Windows version never shipped.

People still search for how to detect Atlas, partly because older logs and fraud reviews mention it and partly because its agent features did not go away. They moved into a browser inside the ChatGPT desktop app, a ChatGPT Chrome extension and a cloud browser that OpenAI runs for agents, and that cloud browser is the part site owners can actually verify. Across sites that use Verisoul, the signed OpenAI cloud browser (ChatGPT agent) made up 13% of the personal-agent sessions we named between Oct 29 and Nov 1, 2026, and it was the most widespread agent after Meta Muse, turning up on about 40% as many customer sites as Muse.
How ChatGPT Atlas showed up on your site

Atlas agent mode ran on the user's own Mac, inside the user's own browser, with their cookies, signed-in sessions and home or office IP. OpenAI never documented a user agent token, request signature or IP list for Atlas traffic, and page requests carried a stock Chrome on macOS user agent with Client Hints that matched Google Chrome, so to a website a visit looked like a person on Chrome for macOS. The one side channel was tab previews, because Atlas fetched `/favicon.ico` for its sidebar with a CFNetwork user agent naming ChatGPT Atlas, which could tag the visit at the network layer even though the page requests were clean. OpenAI's published `chatgpt-user.json` list covers only its separate ChatGPT-User fetcher. The successor cloud browser is a different story, because it runs on OpenAI's side and signs its requests with Web Bot Auth, sending a `Signature-Agent` header for `chatgpt.com` with keys published in OpenAI's key directory, and Cloudflare recognizes it in its [signed agents program](https://blog.cloudflare.com/signed-agents/) under the tag `chatgpt-agent`.

body.text: Why ChatGPT Atlas was hard to detect

Atlas was a real browser on a real person's computer, which removed every signal that usually separates a bot from a customer. There was no datacenter IP, no headless browser and no declared identity, the session cookies belonged to an account the site already trusted, and the agent logic sat outside Chromium instead of being injected into pages as JavaScript, so a page script had nothing to find. The only evidence left was behavior. Researchers at UC Davis studied Atlas in their FP-Agent paper and saw its agent paste text into fields instead of typing, scroll in bursts and move the pointer straight to click targets without the wandering path a hand makes.

The successors split the problem in two. OpenAI's cloud browser is the easy half, since its signature can be verified and it runs on a cloud machine. The browser in the ChatGPT desktop app and the ChatGPT Chrome extension run on the user's own device like Atlas did, and we have not seen OpenAI document a label for either, so they need the same behavioral approach.
How Verisoul detects ChatGPT Atlas and its successors

Verisoul names OpenAI's cloud browser by verifying its Web Bot Auth signature against OpenAI's published `chatgpt.com` key, then checking that the device and the behavior match a cloud agent. A signature can't be copied the way a user agent can, so a `chatgpt_agent` result means the session really came from OpenAI. In-browser sessions, which is what Atlas produced and what the desktop app browser and Chrome extension produce now, carry no signature, so Verisoul flags them through bot score when the behavior is automated and does not name them.

body.text: Should you block ChatGPT Atlas?

Atlas itself no longer sends traffic, so there is nothing to block. For its successors, the signed cloud browser is working for a real ChatGPT user, which is why most teams let it browse and check out and send it to review on sign-up and payouts, where an agent creating accounts or moving money deserves a closer look.

Unsigned in-browser sessions are usually the account holder getting help with an errand. A hard block would turn away real customers, so a high bot score on those sessions works better as a reason to review card changes, payouts and repeated payment attempts than as a reason to stop the session.

body.text: Comet is Perplexity's AI browser, built on Chromium, with an assistant in the sidebar that reads pages, summarizes email and carries out tasks such as shopping inside the user's logged-in sessions. It launched on Jul 9, 2025 for Perplexity Max subscribers at $200 a month, became a free download for everyone on Oct 2, 2025 and now runs on Windows, macOS, Android and iOS. Perplexity said millions of people had joined the waitlist before it went free.

Comet is also the agent at the center of the first big lawsuit over AI shopping. Amazon blocked it on Aug 19, 2025, alleging Perplexity shipped an update within 24 hours to get around the block, and sued on Nov 4, 2025, arguing in its complaint that Comet sends Chrome's user agent with no unique identifier. A preliminary injunction kept Perplexity's agents out of Amazon's password-protected systems from Mar 9, 2026 until the Ninth Circuit vacated it on Aug 4, 2026, holding that the user, not Perplexity, is the one accessing the site. Amazon's other claims are still open, and site owners have been asking how to tell Comet's agent apart from its user ever since.
How Perplexity Comet shows up on your site

Comet runs on the user's own device and talks to your site directly. According to the Ninth Circuit record, screenshots of what the browser shows go to Perplexity's servers, which send back the next navigation steps, while Perplexity's servers never contact the site themselves. Inside the browser, the agent runs through a hidden internal extension, and during agent actions that extension's files, such as `overlay.js`, can show up in the page. Every request still comes from the person's own browser, cookies and IP, with Chrome's user agent and Client Hints. Perplexity publishes IP lists for its PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User fetchers, but those cover different traffic and say nothing about Comet.

body.text: Why Perplexity Comet is hard to detect

Comet is a real Chromium browser on a real customer's device, so it passes the checks that catch most bots. The IP is residential, the cookies belong to an account you already trust and the user agent says Chrome, which Amazon's complaint makes central to its case. Any rule that relies on a declared identity has nothing to match.

What remains is how the assistant behaves when it takes over. Researchers at UC Davis found in their FP-Agent study that Comet pastes text into fields instead of typing, and on Windows it sends Ctrl+A followed by a paste with key holds of about 3 milliseconds. Its turns also show very even timing, dense bursts of actions and a pointer that jumps straight to targets. These traits, and the extension's file names, can change in any Comet update, and the person can take over at any moment, so a single session often mixes human and agent activity.

Verisoul does not name Comet yet, because Comet gives us no declared identity or signature to verify, and we only name an agent when we can prove which one it is. Instead, Verisoul reads the automation that Comet's internal extension leaves in the browser and the machine-like input in the session, and those raise the bot score on the session while the `agent` field stays empty.

body.text: Chrome auto browse is the agent mode of Gemini in Chrome. Google launched it on Jan 28, 2026 as a preview in Chrome desktop for US Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, powered by Gemini 3, and brought it to Android in the US in late June 2026. It takes over the user's browser to finish multi-step tasks such as comparing products, building a cart, booking travel or filling an expense report, and it hands control back to the person to pay, accept terms or create an account.

Google caps usage at 20 tasks a day on AI Pro and 200 on Ultra, so each account sends a limited number of tasks, but it ships inside a browser that Google says has 3.8 billion users. In late July 2026 Google also connected its Gemini Spark agent to auto browse, which can use logged-in accounts and saved passwords with the user's permission. That combination of reach and access to real accounts is why fraud and risk teams want to know when it is on their site.
How Chrome auto browse shows up on your site

Auto browse mostly runs in the user's own signed-in Chrome on their desktop or Android phone, with their cookies and IP, and the device has to stay awake while it works. In that mode it sends no agent token and no signature, so a site sees a normal Chrome visit. Google's help page adds that Gemini may switch to a remote browser in the cloud when the device is unavailable, and those tasks pause at sign-in steps.

Google also runs a declared identity for agents on its own infrastructure, called Google-Agent, which it added to its crawler docs on Mar 20, 2026. It carries `compatible; Google-Agent` in the user agent, comes from IPs in Google's published `user-triggered-agents.json` list and is part of a Web Bot Auth experiment under the identity `agent.bot.goog`. Google has not said whether auto browse's cloud browser uses it, which is the most important open question on this page.

body.text: OpenClaw is an open-source personal AI agent that runs on the user's own computer or server, takes instructions over chat apps such as WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack and iMessage, and uses a real browser to get things done with the user's accounts. Peter Steinberger first published it on Nov 24, 2025 under the name Warelay, and it went through CLAWDIS, Clawdbot and Moltbot before settling on OpenClaw on Jan 30, 2026. In February Steinberger joined OpenAI, and the project moved to the OpenClaw Foundation, a non-profit OpenAI supports, while the code stays MIT-licensed.

Its growth has been unusual even by AI standards. The New Stack reported that OpenClaw passed React in early March 2026 to become GitHub's most-starred software project, and the [repository](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw) showed 393.5k stars and 82.7k forks on Nov 1, 2026. Tom's Hardware reported 1.5 million agents created by early February. OpenClaw 2.0 shipped on Aug 30, 2026 with easier setup and shared cloud sessions, which lowers the bar for people who would never have touched a terminal.

For fraud and risk teams the interest comes from what OpenClaw can do once it has a browser. It fills forms, signs up for accounts, books, shops and posts, and nothing in the core project forces a human approval before a purchase. Third-party skills openly teach anti-bot bypass, so the same tool that runs one person's errands can also run a sign-up farm.
How OpenClaw shows up on your site

By default, OpenClaw's local Gateway launches a dedicated agent-only Chrome, Brave, Edge or Chromium profile and drives it over the Chrome DevTools Protocol with Playwright on top, according to its [browser tool docs](https://docs.openclaw.ai/tools/browser). On a Linux server with no display it goes headless automatically. Users can also attach it to their real, signed-in Chrome through Chrome DevTools MCP or a relay extension, or point it at a hosted browser from a vendor such as Browserbase or Browser Use, and each of those changes what your site sees.

body.text: Why OpenClaw is easy to catch in some setups and hard in others

The default setup is the easy case, because a fresh Playwright-driven profile over CDP leaves automation artifacts in the browser, a headless server run can announce HeadlessChrome, and an agent-only profile arrives with no history or cookies, so it looks like a brand new device on every run. Playwright also tends to leave its own globals in the page, such as `__playwright__binding__` and `__pwInitScripts`. Those are the same markers any scripted browser leaves, and they are reliable when present.

The hard case is attached mode. When OpenClaw rides the user's own Chrome on their home connection, the fingerprint, cookies and IP all belong to a real person, and the only thing left is how the session behaves. Self-hosting also means there is no central egress and no shared identity, while every user's mix of skills and backends is different, so no single list or rule covers OpenClaw as a whole.
How Verisoul detects OpenClaw

Verisoul does not name OpenClaw itself, because OpenClaw never declares who it is. What we name is the automation it uses. When OpenClaw drives its own browser, the browser gives itself away through DevTools-protocol automation artifacts or headless markers in the device fingerprint, and the session moves with scripted navigation and no human input. Verisoul returns those sessions as `cdp_automation` or `headless_chrome`. When it attaches to the user's real Chrome, Verisoul flags the session through bot score and does not name the agent.

body.text: Browser Use is an MIT-licensed Python library that lets a large language model drive a Chromium browser by turning each page into structured text the model can act on. Magnus Muller and Gregor Zunic first showed it on Hacker News as a weekend prototype in late 2024, and by Mar 22, 2025 it had 50,000 GitHub stars and a $17M seed round led by Felicis, with Y Combinator, Paul Graham and SV Angel joining. The [repository](https://github.com/browser-use/browser-use) had about 119,200 stars on Nov 1, 2026.

The company also sells Browser Use Cloud, which rents stealth cloud browsers and runs hosted web agents. Browser Use says its cloud created 3.7M browser sessions in the seven days to Oct 14, 2026, which is a vendor figure but gives a sense of scale. It is also the browser layer under other agents, including Hermes Agent and some of OpenAI's computer-use hosting partners, so its traffic often carries someone else's agent.

Site owners ask about it because it is the default way developers point an LLM at a website. Logins, form filling, booking and checkout flows are all documented use cases, and the cloud product markets getting through bot protection as a feature.
How Browser Use shows up on your site

Since Aug 20, 2025 the library has controlled Chromium directly over the Chrome DevTools Protocol rather than through Playwright, as the team explains in [leaving Playwright for CDP](https://browser-use.com/posts/playwright-to-cdp). A self-hosted run therefore looks like a CDP-driven Chromium coming from wherever the developer runs it, often a cloud VM. Browser Use Cloud is different, because it runs a hardened Chromium fork with stealth on by default, fingerprints randomized per session, residential proxies in 195+ countries and automatic CAPTCHA solving outside its EU region, per its [stealth docs](https://docs.browser-use.com/cloud/browser/stealth).

body.text: Why Browser Use is hard to detect

There is nothing declared to match, which means every check has to come from the browser and the behavior. Self-hosted runs are the easier half, because CDP control leaves automation artifacts and the sessions often come from datacenter IPs on VM hardware. The cloud fork is built to remove exactly those tells, and because it randomizes canvas, WebGL, font and navigator fingerprints on every session while exiting through residential IPs, static checks mostly come up empty.

Behavior is harder to fake. A May 2026 academic study, [FP-Agent](https://arxiv.org/html/2605.01247v1), found that Browser Use typed with near-constant gaps between keystrokes, moved the cursor by jumping straight to targets with no movement in between, and scrolled in instant jumps, which separated it from people almost perfectly. The same study found its fingerprint often matched other agents, so fingerprints alone were a weaker way to tell agents apart than behavior was.
How Verisoul detects Browser Use

For self-hosted runs, Verisoul labels the session by what the browser reveals about itself: DevTools-protocol automation artifacts in the browser, plus scripted navigation with no human input. Those sessions come back as `cdp_automation`. Browser Use Cloud stealth sessions are flagged through bot score, and Verisoul does not yet name Browser Use as the agent.

It runs on the user's computer or server, keeps long-term memory, writes reusable skills from tasks it has already done, and takes actions, including browsing, on command from chat apps like Telegram, Slack and WhatsApp. Tech Times dates its public launch to Feb 25, 2026, and it is MIT-licensed on macOS, Windows, Linux and Android, with optional Nous Portal cloud plans.

Those saved skills are what make Hermes interesting to a fraud team. Once a skill exists for a site, running the same task again is cheap, which is great for one person's weekly errand and just as useful to someone repeating the same sign-up or listing flow hundreds of times.
How Hermes Agent shows up on your site

Hermes has no web identity of its own, so what reaches you is whatever browser it is configured to use. Its [browser docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser) list a local headless Chromium with a throwaway profile as the default. It can instead snapshot the user's real browser profile, attach to their own Chrome, Edge or Brave over the DevTools Protocol, or use cloud browsers from Browserbase, Browser Use, Firecrawl or the Nous Tool Gateway. Before Mar 7, 2026, browsing required a Browserbase key, so early Hermes traffic came through Browserbase.

Browserbase was in Cloudflare's first cohort of signed agents in Aug 2025, so its signed sessions can be verified, while unsigned ones leave behavior as the main tell: instant typing, no mouse movement and burst scrolling. body.text: Computer-use APIs are model endpoints that look at a screenshot and reply with the next mouse click or keystroke, so a developer's own program can operate a browser or desktop on a user's behalf. Anthropic released computer use in public beta with Claude 3.5 Sonnet on [Oct 22, 2024](https://www.anthropic.com/news/3-5-models-and-computer-use). OpenAI followed on Mar 11, 2025 with its Computer-Using Agent model in the Responses API, and Google released the Gemini 2.5 Computer Use model, tuned for browsers, on Oct 7, 2025.

None of the three vendors publishes usage numbers for these APIs, which makes them hard to size. What we know is that they are paid per token and that the developer supplies and pays for the browser or desktop the model controls. That second part is what matters for detection, because the AI company never touches your site at all.

Developers use them for form filling and data entry, testing user flows, booking and shopping tasks, scraping behind logins and back-office workflows. Any site with a form or a login can see them, and they turn up most on SaaS sign-ups, ecommerce and travel.
How computer-use agents show up on your site

The model only returns actions, and the developer's code carries them out in a browser the developer runs. Anthropic's [reference implementation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool) is a Docker container with a virtual Linux desktop and Firefox. OpenAI's [samples](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/tools-computer-use) use Playwright with local Chromium and list Browserbase, Browser Use, Daytona and E2B as hosted partners, while Google's [samples](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/computer-use) use Playwright Chromium at 1440x900. Traffic leaves from the developer's VM, laptop or browser host, not from Anthropic, OpenAI or Google.

body.text: Why computer-use agents are easy to catch in default setups

The reference setups are built for clarity, not stealth. Playwright Chromium and a virtual Linux desktop in Docker leave automation markers, VM traits and datacenter IPs. Playwright tends to leave globals such as `__playwright__binding__` and `__pwInitScripts` in the page, and WebDriver harnesses built on ChromeDriver leave `cdc_` variables in the document, and the way the model works adds its own rhythm: a fixed, round viewport, long pauses while the model reads each screenshot, then a single click with the cursor jumping straight to its target, and text that arrives pasted or perfectly even.

All of that depends on the host. When a developer runs the same model on a stealth browser service with residential proxies, the automation markers disappear and only the pacing remains, while a host that signs, such as Browserbase, which Cloudflare lists as a signed agent, identifies itself instead. That is why the same Claude, OpenAI or Gemini agent can be trivial to catch in one deployment and hard in the next.
How Verisoul detects computer-use agents

body.text: Browserbase runs hosted headless browsers for developers' AI agents, along with tools on top such as the Stagehand framework and Director, a no-code product for web tasks. The company was founded in Jan 2024 by Paul Klein IV, launched its platform that year, and raised a $40M Series B led by Notable Capital in Jun 2025. Its homepage says 10,000+ companies build on it, which is a vendor figure, and it is also the browser host underneath many other agents, from Hermes Agent users to demos of the big computer-use models.

Browserbase has also become one of the more visible voices on agent identity. Cloudflare named it in its [first cohort of signed agents](https://blog.cloudflare.com/signed-agents/) on Aug 28, 2025, and Cloudflare Radar lists it as a verified agent with an HTTP message signatures directory. On Apr 6, 2026 it launched [Agent Identity](https://www.browserbase.com/blog/identity) and Verified sessions with Cloudflare and 1Password, the latter giving agents stored credentials. That makes it one of the few hosted browsers whose traffic can prove where it came from.

Site owners care because Browserbase traffic reaches logged-in flows, ecommerce orders and form-heavy pages, often on behalf of a customer the site has never heard of. Knowing that a session came from Browserbase is useful, while knowing which of its customers sent it is not something any check can tell you. The Perplexity dispute in Aug 2025 showed the problem: after Cloudflare reported that Perplexity was using an undeclared crawler posing as Chrome on macOS, [Perplexity said](https://www.techradar.com/pro/perplexity-hits-back-after-cloudflare-slams-its-online-scraping-tools) much of that traffic came from Browserbase, which shows how hard unsigned hosted sessions are to attribute.

Hermes Agent's [browser docs](https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/docs/user-guide/features/browser) describe Browserbase's basic stealth, with random fingerprints and CAPTCHA solving, as always on.

Browserbase's [Agent Identity docs](https://docs.browserbase.com/platform/identity/overview) describe Web Bot Auth signing as a beta that customers request, even though Cloudflare already treats Browserbase as a signed agent, which means Cloudflare customers can allow or block it by name in their bot settings. body.text: Puppeteer is a Node.js library from Google's Chrome DevTools team that drives Chrome or Chromium over the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so code can load pages, click, type and read results without a person. It was first released on Aug 16, 2017, reached 1.0 in Jan 2018, and is free under Apache 2.0. In the week of Oct 23 to Oct 29, 2026, npm counted 15.4M downloads of `puppeteer` and 31.8M of `puppeteer-core`, the version without a bundled browser.

Most of that is testing, screenshots and PDF rendering. The same library also powers scraping, account creation bots and credential stuffing, and many AI agent stacks still sit on the DevTools Protocol that Puppeteer made popular. One more number says a lot about how it gets used: `puppeteer-extra-plugin-stealth`, a plugin built to hide Puppeteer's automation markers, still drew about 1.5M weekly downloads in the same week despite no release since Mar 2023.
How Puppeteer and headless Chrome show up on your site

Puppeteer launches Chrome for Testing in new headless mode by default since v22 (Feb 5, 2024), or the older `chrome-headless-shell` binary with `headless: 'shell'`. Chrome removed old headless from Chrome 132 and ships it only as that separate binary, as [Chrome for Developers](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/removing-headless-old-from-chrome) explains. The difference matters for detection, because old headless puts HeadlessChrome in the user agent and `sec-ch-ua`, while [new headless](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/chromium/new-headless) shares the regular Chrome codebase and sends a normal Chrome token.

body.text: Why Puppeteer is easy to catch until someone hides it

Stock Puppeteer is easy to catch, because `navigator.webdriver` is true, DevTools-protocol control leaves automation artifacts, shell mode announces HeadlessChrome, the sessions usually come from datacenter IPs, and a Chromium browser that sends no Accept-Language header is a classic headless tell. Those checks hold up well against careless scripts.

Each of them can be removed. New headless already drops the user agent token, the Chrome flag `--disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled` turns off the webdriver flag, a custom user agent hides the rest, and residential proxies take care of the IP. New headless also shares the regular Chrome codebase, so most of the JavaScript fingerprint differences that used to give headless away are gone, and a well-known DevTools probe that relied on a custom stack getter stopped working after V8 changes in May 2025. body.text: Playwright is Microsoft's open source library for scripting real browsers. It drives Chromium, Firefox and WebKit from JavaScript, Python, C# and Java, and it shipped 1.0 on npm on May 6, 2020. It started as a testing tool and still is one, while a growing share of its traffic now comes from scrapers and from AI agents that need a browser to operate websites.

The numbers show how common it has become. The [playwright npm package](https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/playwright) logged 154.5M downloads in the week of Oct 23 to Oct 29, 2026, and the [Python package](https://pypistats.org/api/packages/playwright/recent) about 30.4M in the week to Nov 1. [Playwright MCP](https://api.npmjs.org/downloads/point/last-week/@playwright/mcp), the server that hands the same engine to LLM agents through accessibility snapshots, added another 8.6M weekly npm downloads, which is why a Playwright session on your sign-up page today is as likely to be an agent as a test.
How Playwright shows up on your site

Playwright is a library, so it runs wherever the operator puts it: a developer laptop, a CI runner, a cloud VM or a hosted browser grid. It downloads its own browser builds, and since [version 1.49](https://github.com/microsoft/playwright/issues/33566) (Nov 18, 2024) default headless Chromium runs as chromium-headless-shell, which carries the HeadlessChrome marker in its user agent. Nothing about the network gives it away on its own, because the IP is whatever the operator rents. The library never signs requests, though some hosted browser companies that run Playwright sessions can, and Browserbase and Anchor Browser were in the first group of [Cloudflare signed agents](https://blog.cloudflare.com/signed-agents/) in Aug 2025.

Some agent frameworks have also left Playwright entirely. [Browser Use moved to raw DevTools-protocol control](https://browser-use.com/posts/playwright-to-cdp) in Aug 2025, so its sessions show no Playwright-specific traces even though they are still automated. A check that looks for Playwright by name will miss these, while a check for DevTools automation and scripted behavior still catches them.

body.text: Selenium is an open source project, a member of the Software Freedom Conservancy, that controls real browsers through language bindings and per-browser drivers such as ChromeDriver and geckodriver. It powers a large share of automated testing, and the same code drives sneaker bots, appointment bots and survey farms.

It remains widely installed. Teams usually ask about it after a wave of scripted sign-ups or bookings, because it is the first tool many bot operators learn.
How Selenium shows up on your site

Selenium runs the real browser, so the user agent is the real Chrome, Firefox, Edge or Safari string, and old-style headless Chrome may still show HeadlessChrome. The tell sits inside the browser: the [W3C WebDriver spec](https://www.w3.org/TR/webdriver2/) has the browser set navigator.webdriver to true whenever WebDriver is in control, which makes automation something the browser is supposed to announce. Selenium 4 also exposes DevTools and BiDi features for Chromium and Firefox.

body.text: Why Selenium is easy to detect

Stock Selenium declares itself by standard, because the webdriver flag is set by the browser and ChromeDriver adds its own `cdc_` variables to the document, such as `document.$cdc_asdjflasutopfhvcZLmcfl_`, which may only appear after the script first interacts with the page. A script on your site can read both in a few lines, which makes the default setup the easiest of the automation libraries to catch.

Operators know this, which is why [undetected-chromedriver](https://pypi.org/project/undetected-chromedriver/) still gets about 605,700 weekly downloads even though its last release, 3.5.5, came out on Feb 17, 2024. It patches ChromeDriver to remove the flag and the `cdc_` variables, and others get the same result by recompiling or hex-editing the driver, while the project's own page warns that it does not hide your IP. Once those markers are gone, the session still behaves like a script and often still arrives from a datacenter, so detection moves to behavior and network.

Selenium doesn't sign anything or publish an identity, so Verisoul reads what the browser declares. Our SDK checks for the WebDriver automation flag and driver artifacts in the browser, then pairs that with session behavior, where scripted navigation with no human input stands out. Any browser under WebDriver control comes back under the same id, whichever language binding launched it.

body.text: OpenAI documents four bots on its [crawler overview](https://developers.openai.com/docs/bots). GPTBot collects public pages that may be used to train models, OAI-SearchBot indexes pages for ChatGPT search, ChatGPT-User fetches a page live when a ChatGPT user, Custom GPT or GPT Action asks for it, and OAI-AdsBot checks the landing pages of ads shown in ChatGPT. The oldest is ChatGPT-User, which arrived with [ChatGPT plugins](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-plugins/) on Mar 23, 2023, and GPTBot followed on Aug 7, 2023.

Site owners see a lot of this traffic. In Cloudflare Radar data for July 2026, GPTBot made up 9.7% of AI-bot traffic, ahead of OAI-SearchBot at 1.6% and ChatGPT-User at 1.3%, and [Cloudflare found](https://blog.cloudflare.com/from-googlebot-to-gptbot-whos-crawling-your-site-in-2025/) that ChatGPT-User requests grew 2,825% from May 2024 to May 2025 while GPTBot requests grew 305%. GPTBot was also the AI bot most often disallowed in robots.txt among top domains in June 2025. Publishers want to decide what feeds training and what feeds search, and since Dec 9, 2025 OpenAI's docs say robots.txt rules [may not apply to ChatGPT-User](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/openai-says-robots-txt-may-not-apply-to-chatgpts-fetch-bot/585864/), because a person started the fetch.
How OpenAI's bots show up on your site

All four are server-side HTTP fetchers that run from fixed IP prefixes OpenAI publishes in one JSON file per bot. On Nov 1, 2026 the ChatGPT-User list held 235 prefixes, OAI-SearchBot 39, GPTBot 18 and OAI-AdsBot 2, and the ChatGPT-User list changes often. Each request carries a short token with an openai.com link, such as `GPTBot/1.4` or `ChatGPT-User/1.0`.

guides.answer: You detect Perplexity's declared bots by matching the PerplexityBot/1.0 or Perplexity-User/1.0 token in the user agent and confirming the IP is in the matching JSON file Perplexity publishes. Both identify themselves, but Cloudflare reported on Aug 4, 2025 that Perplexity also fetched blocked sites with an undeclared agent posing as Chrome on macOS from unlisted IPs, which Perplexity disputes and which a token and IP check cannot catch. body.text: Perplexity's [crawler docs](https://docs.perplexity.ai/docs/resources/perplexity-crawlers) list two bots. PerplexityBot indexes pages so they can surface and be cited in Perplexity's answers, and Perplexity says it is not used to train foundation models. Perplexity-User fetches a page live when a user's question needs it, from the web, the apps or the API. Perplexity has not published a launch date for either.

Site owners ask about Perplexity more than most because of its history. In June 2024 [Wired traced an unlisted Perplexity IP on AWS](https://www.wired.com/story/perplexity-is-a-bullshit-machine/) fetching Condé Nast pages that had blocked PerplexityBot, and a year later Cloudflare made a larger version of the same claim.
Cloudflare's stealth crawling report and Perplexity's response

On Aug 4, 2025 [Cloudflare reported](https://blog.cloudflare.com/perplexity-is-using-stealth-undeclared-crawlers-to-evade-website-no-crawl-directives/) that when its customers blocked PerplexityBot and Perplexity-User, Perplexity kept fetching their pages with an undeclared agent that posed as Chrome on macOS and rotated through IPs and networks outside Perplexity's published lists. Cloudflare set up brand-new test domains that disallowed all bots and still saw their content in Perplexity's answers. It measured 20 to 25 million daily requests from Perplexity's declared agents and 3 to 6 million from the undeclared one, removed Perplexity from its verified bots program and added the stealth crawler to its managed AI crawler rule, including on free plans.

Perplexity disputed the report. It said on X that Cloudflare had misattributed traffic from BrowserBase, a hosted browser service it says it uses for fewer than 45,000 requests a day, and argued that agents fetching pages for a user's question are not bots and need not follow robots.txt, a position [Search Engine Journal](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/cloudflare-delists-and-blocks-perplexity-from-crawling-websites/552899/) and [TechRadar](https://www.techradar.com/pro/perplexity-hits-back-after-cloudflare-slams-its-online-scraping-tools) covered at the time. We found no public sign that Cloudflare has restored Perplexity's verified bot status.
How Perplexity's bots show up on your site

Both bots are HTTP fetchers that send a Chrome-like WebKit user agent with a declared token and a perplexity.ai link, such as `PerplexityBot/1.0` or `Perplexity-User/1.0`. They come from IP ranges Perplexity publishes in two files, [perplexitybot.json](https://www.perplexity.com/perplexitybot.json) and [perplexity-user.json](https://www.perplexity.com/perplexity-user.json), which Perplexity calls the source of truth. Neither signs its requests, and Perplexity was not among the first [Cloudflare signed agents](https://blog.cloudflare.com/signed-agents/). Comet, Perplexity's AI browser, is a separate product that looks like a normal browser.

Meta-ExternalAgent was quietly documented in July 2024, and [Fortune reported it on Aug 20, 2024](https://fortune.com/2024/08/20/meta-external-agent-new-web-crawler-bot-scrape-data-train-ai-models-llama). It grew quickly from there, from about 0.9% to about 7.5% of crawler traffic between July 2024 and July 2025, and in Cloudflare Radar data for July 2026 it made up about 12.7% of AI-bot traffic, second only to Googlebot.

Meta's agent traffic is a different story. Across sites that use Verisoul, from Oct 29 to Nov 1, 2026 (Nov 1 partial), Meta's personal agent Muse made up 68% of the personal-agent sessions we named and produced roughly 20 times as many sessions as Meta-ExternalAds, even though Muse uses none of these tokens.
How Meta's bots show up on your site

All of them are HTTP crawlers and fetchers that run from Meta's own network, AS32934, each with a short declared user agent such as `meta-externalagent/1.1` or `facebookexternalhit/1.1`. Meta does not publish a JSON IP list and instead points site owners to a RADb whois lookup for AS32934, warning that the IPs change often.

body.text: Why Meta's bots are easy to detect

Every bot declares a Meta token and all of the traffic comes from Meta's own network, so spoofing is easy to spot, which matters because scrapers often fake facebookexternalhit to get past sites that allowlist link previews. The friction is that there is no signature or IP file, so verification means a whois lookup you have to keep fresh.

Robots.txt only goes so far. Meta-ExternalAgent and Meta-WebIndexer respect it, with changes taking up to 24 hours, while Meta-ExternalFetcher may bypass it for user requests and facebookexternalhit may bypass it for security and integrity checks. Meta's in-app browsers carry real people and are not these bots at all, and Muse reports as desktop Chrome on Linux and exits through large CDN networks rather than consumer ISPs or AS32934, so these checks don't reach either.
How Verisoul detects Meta's bots

The bots are self-declared, so Verisoul reads the token and confirms the source IP belongs to Meta's own network before naming it. A Meta token from anywhere else is a spoofer. Muse is a separate case that we name by inference from its hosting network, device and behavior, and it has its own guide.

body.text: Should you block Meta's bots?

These bots read pages and build previews, so allowing them is a content decision rather than a fraud one. Most teams keep facebookexternalhit allowed, decide on Meta-ExternalAgent by training policy, and block any Meta token that doesn't come from Meta's network.

faq.q: What is meta-externalagent and should I block it?
faq.a: It is Meta's crawler for training AI models and indexing content for Meta products, and it was about 12.7% of AI-bot traffic on Cloudflare in July 2026. It follows robots.txt, so block it there if you don't want your pages used for training.

faq.q: Will blocking facebookexternalhit break link previews?
faq.a: Yes. facebookexternalhit builds the preview when someone shares your URL on Facebook, Instagram or Messenger, so keep it allowed and verify it comes from Meta's network instead.

faq.q: Does Meta respect robots.txt for AI training?
faq.a: Meta says Meta-ExternalAgent and Meta-WebIndexer respect robots.txt, with changes taking up to 24 hours. Meta-ExternalFetcher and facebookexternalhit may bypass it.

faq.q: How do I get Meta crawler IP addresses?
faq.a: Meta doesn't publish a JSON list. It tells site owners to query RADb for routes announced by AS32934 and warns the IPs change often.

faq.q: Is Meta Muse one of these crawlers?
faq.a: No. Muse is Meta's personal AI agent and does not use these tokens. Verisoul names it separately as meta_muse.
